### Exercise: Evaluating the new instructions

::: {.exercise}
**Part I: run Gemma with the new instructions**

Classify all headlines again with Gemma, but now using the new `instruction` we created earlier.
You can base yourself on the code from @sec-llm-validation,
but you only need to run a single model.

Complete the `mutate` function below, 
but note that you have to use the same prompt template as before
with the new `instruction` as answers are pre-computed in this interactive exercise.
`instruction` is available as an object in this code so you don't need to copy/paste it. 

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_codebook_run
library(tidyverse)
headlines <- read_csv("data/dutch_sentiment.csv")
{{< include exercises/_llm_mock.qmd >}}

library(ellmer)
codes <- c(
  positive = "the headline evaluates the economy or economic conditions as good or improving",
  negative = "the headline evaluates the economy or economic conditions as bad or worsening",
  neutral = "the headline gives no evaluation of economic conditions, or is ambiguous or mixed")
codebook <- str_glue("- {names(codes)} = {codes}") |> str_c(collapse="\n")
task <- "You are classifying newspaper headlines by their sentiment about the economy, as in a content analysis of economic news."
context <- "Judge only the headline itself, not anything else you may know about the events it refers to."
answer <- "Answer with only one word, in lowercase: positive, negative, or neutral."
instruction <- str_glue("{task} {context}\n\nCodebook:\n{codebook}\n\n{answer}")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_codebook_run
#| warning: false
chat_gemma <- chat_ollama(model = "gemma4:e4b")

results_codebook <- headlines |>
  mutate()
head(results_codebook)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_codebook_run"}
::: { .callout-tip title="Hint:"}
1. Use `interpolate` to create the prompt using the same template as before: `"{{instruction}}\n\nThe headline: {{headline}}"`.
2. Use `parallel_chat_text` with the chat object and the prompts.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_codebook_run"}
::: { .callout-important icon=false title="🎓 Solution:"}
This is the same code as in @sec-llm-validation, but with only one model.
The template is also unchanged: because the new instructions are stored in a variable with the same name,
`interpolate` automatically uses them.
This is a nice benefit of building the prompt from separate parts:
you can change the instructions without touching the code that runs the classification.

Note that the template must match exactly,
since we can only replay the answers that were recorded for these exact prompts.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_codebook_run
#| solution: true
#| warning: false
chat_gemma <- chat_ollama(model = "gemma4:e4b")

results_codebook <- headlines |>
  mutate(
    prompts = interpolate("{{instruction}}\n\nThe headline: {{headline}}"),
    llm_gemma = parallel_chat_text(chat_gemma, prompts)
  )
head(results_codebook)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_codebook_run
#| check: true

gradethis::grade_this({
  results_codebook <- .envir_result$results_codebook
  if (is.data.frame(results_codebook)) {
    gradethis::fail_if(
      !"llm_gemma" %in% names(results_codebook),
      "Your `results_codebook` has no `llm_gemma` column. Did you store the answers under that name?")
    gradethis::fail_if(
      anyNA(results_codebook$llm_gemma),
      "Some headlines have no answer. Did you use the model `\"gemma4:e4b\"`, and exactly the same template as before, `\"{{instruction}}\\n\\nThe headline: {{headline}}\"`?")
  }

  {{< include exercises/_check.qmd >}}
})
```

**Part II: evaluate the result**

Due to how exercises work in this interactive textbook,
we will work from the results of the previous exercise,
regardless of whether you managed to solve it or not.

So, you can start from the `results_codebook` dataframe, which
has a `sentiment` column and `llm_gemma` column per headline.

Compute the accuracy for this model by computing the proportion of headlines
for which Gemma gave the correct answer. 
Next, show the confusion matrix, i.e. a 
data frame with the gold standard sentiment in the rows,
Gemma's sentiment in the columns,
and frequencies in the cells. 

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_codebook_accuracy
library(tidyverse)
headlines <- read_csv("data/dutch_sentiment.csv")
{{< include exercises/_llm_mock.qmd >}}

library(ellmer)
codes <- c(
  positive = "the headline evaluates the economy or economic conditions as good or improving",
  negative = "the headline evaluates the economy or economic conditions as bad or worsening",
  neutral = "the headline gives no evaluation of economic conditions, or is ambiguous or mixed")
codebook <- str_glue("- {names(codes)} = {codes}") |> str_c(collapse="\n")
task <- "You are classifying newspaper headlines by their sentiment about the economy, as in a content analysis of economic news."
context <- "Judge only the headline itself, not anything else you may know about the events it refers to."
answer <- "Answer with only one word, in lowercase: positive, negative, or neutral."
instruction <- str_glue("{task} {context}\n\nCodebook:\n{codebook}\n\n{answer}")
# Looks the answers up in the recordings directly, rather than replaying all of them through ellmer, which takes a while
cached_answers <- function(model, prompts) {
  llm_recorded$answer[match(llm_key(model, "", prompts), llm_recorded_keys)]
}
results_codebook <- headlines |>
  mutate(
    prompts = interpolate("{{instruction}}\n\nThe headline: {{headline}}"),
    llm_llama = cached_answers("llama3.2:3b", prompts),
    llm_haiku = cached_answers("claude-haiku-4-5", prompts),
    llm_gemma = cached_answers("gemma4:e4b", prompts),
    llm_nano = cached_answers("gpt-4.1-nano", prompts)
  )
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_codebook_accuracy
#| warning: false
# Compute and print accuracy
accuracy <- ...
cat("Overall accuracy:\n")
accuracy

cat("\nConfusion matrix:\n")
results_codebook |> ...
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_codebook_accuracy"}
::: { .callout-tip title="Hint:"}
- For accuracy, you can summarize the mean of whether the two columns are the same (since there is only one model, no need to group_by here)
- For the confusion matrix, count the frequency of each `sentiment` and `llm_gemma` pair, and then `pivot_wider` to create the table.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_codebook_accuracy"}
::: { .callout-important icon=false title="🎓 Solution:"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_codebook_accuracy
#| solution: true
#| warning: false
# Compute and print accuracy
accuracy <- results_codebook |>
  summarize(accuracy=mean(sentiment == llm_gemma))
cat("Overall accuracy:\n")
accuracy

cat("\nConfusion matrix:\n")
results_codebook |>
  group_by(sentiment, llm_gemma) |>
  summarize(value=n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_wider(names_from=llm_gemma)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_codebook_accuracy
#| check: true

gradethis::grade_this({
  # Accept the accuracy as a number, a 1x1 tibble from summarize, or as a percentage
  correct_accuracy <- mean(results_codebook$sentiment == results_codebook$llm_gemma)
  accuracy <- .envir_result$accuracy
  accuracy_value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(unlist(accuracy)))
  gradethis::fail_if(
    is.null(accuracy),
    "Did you store the accuracy in a variable called `accuracy`?")
  gradethis::fail_if(
    length(accuracy_value) != 1 || is.na(accuracy_value) ||
      !(isTRUE(all.equal(accuracy_value, correct_accuracy)) ||
        isTRUE(all.equal(accuracy_value, 100 * correct_accuracy))),
    "Your `accuracy` is not quite right. It should be a single number: the mean of the comparison between `sentiment` and `llm_gemma`.")

  if (is.data.frame(.result)) {
    gradethis::fail_if(
      !"sentiment" %in% names(.result),
      "The rows of the confusion matrix should be the gold standard: make sure you group by `sentiment` as well as by `llm_gemma`.")
    gradethis::fail_if(
      !all(c("positive", "negative", "neutral") %in% names(.result)),
      "The answers of Gemma should be the columns of the confusion matrix. Did you use `pivot_wider` with `names_from=llm_gemma`?")
    gradethis::fail_if(
      dplyr::is_grouped_df(.result),
      "Your confusion matrix looks right, but it is still grouped. Add `ungroup()` before `pivot_wider`.")
  }

  {{< include exercises/_check.qmd >}}
})
```
:::

::: {.challenge title="Did the codebook help?"}
- Compare the accuracy of Gemma with the new instructions to the accuracy we found in @sec-llm-validation.
  Did the codebook help?
- Compare the confusion matrix to the one we made for Gemma before.
  Where does the improvement come from? Did we fix the problem with the neutral category,
  and did that come at a cost for the other categories?
- The `results_codebook` actually also contains the results of the other models, e.g. in `llm_nano`. Can you look at the accuracy of the other models as well? Does the new codebook help them too?
- Can you make a confusion matrix for the nano model? What is your diagnosis?
- What do these results tell you about whether there is a single 'best' prompt?
- On your own computer, with a real LLM (see @sec-llm-api and @sec-ollama), try to improve the instructions further.
  For example, you could add decision rules for difficult cases, or give an example for each category.
  Does it help? Does it help for all models?
:::
